planting.note: Scatter seed over bare, lightly raked soil in autumn and let winter rain do the germinating; performs best where the soil surface has been scraped or disturbed.

directions: A tiny-flowered but exceptionally high-value pollinator annual, this cryptantha draws well over 200 native bee species plus numerous butterflies and moths, serving as a larval host for painted lady butterflies. Site it in full sun on fast-draining, lean soil, since overwatering or rich soil produces lanky, floppy growth with fewer flowers. Because it's such a heavy pollinator draw, interplanting it along the edges of a vegetable or orchard bed can help support shared pollinators for crops like stone fruit.

planting.note: Direct-sow onto open, dry ground in fall without crowding it with lush perennials or heavy mulch; let it self-sow in a dry meadow or gravel garden.

directions: Strong pollinator-garden value and tolerant of the widest elevation range in this group, from sea level to 6,000 feet, across chaparral, foothill woodland, valley grassland, and yellow pine forest, this cryptantha is a genuinely adaptable filler species for naturalistic dry-garden plantings across much of California. Grow it as a matrix species scattered thinly through a dry meadow rather than as a feature plant, since individual flowers are tiny and the display is cumulative rather than showy. Established populations persist via seed bank through dry years.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall under open oak or pine canopy into sandy or gravelly, fast-draining soil; avoid soil amendment or irrigation beyond establishment watering.

directions: Notably the one Cryptantha in this group that genuinely prefers partial shade rather than full sun, this species occupies chaparral understory, foothill woodland, and open conifer forest, making it a candidate for the dry, shaded fringe of an oak or pine woodland garden where full-sun wildflowers fail. Its bristly, hairy fruiting stems and small white flowers are more textural than showy, so it reads best as groundcover filler rather than a focal planting. Bloom extends into summer, later than most sun-loving cryptanthas.
sources: San Diego State University (Simpson & Hasenstab, Crossosoma)

planting.note: Direct-sow onto sandy or gravelly open ground in fall; treat as an experimental crevice or scree-garden filler since documented cultivation information is thin.

directions: A true miniature mat-forming cushion annual rarely exceeding four inches tall, this cryptantha fills a texture niche for rock gardens or gravel-garden crevices that no other candidate in this group does, with the broadest climate range in the genus from Washington to Baja California to Colorado. It thrives on neglect: sandy or gravelly, nutrient-poor soil with zero supplemental water once established. Best trialed in a dedicated gravel bed rather than relied upon for a design feature, since it disappears if planted among anything taller.

planting.note: Direct-sow over prepared bare soil in fall and give a deep winter soak, then withhold water entirely through spring; tolerates clay, loam, rocky, or sandy soil.

directions: Unlike the vernal-pool and grassland species already in the collection, this popcornflower tolerates clay, loam, rocky, or sandy soil, unusual flexibility for this group, and is documented to last all spring without supplemental water once established, attracting butterflies. It is built to finish its whole life cycle on stored winter moisture. Pair it with the already-present popcorn flower in a mixed drift for a longer, layered bloom display across a dry meadow.

planting.note: Scatter seed thinly onto bare soil in fall without burying it, since it germinates best on or near the soil surface with light exposure.

directions: A taller, more erect habit than the low-growing popcorn flower already in the collection, this species gives a genuinely distinct vertical layer for a popcornflower-themed wildflower drift, common in foothill woodland and valley grassland communities. Place it toward the back of a dry meadow drift where its small white-and-purple flowers read as airy texture rather than a solid carpet. It completes its cycle and dies back completely by early summer, so plan a drought-dormant companion to carry the space through the dry season.
